title: Idleness is the enemy (ch. 48)
hookLine: pray and work, balanced through the day

lines: ORA ET LABORA. PRAY AND WORK.
cards: Three short Latin words: ora et labora. Pray and work. Some people use them to sum up a Benedictine life in a breath.
After yesterday, it might seem the monks did nothing but drop their tools and run to chapel. They didn't.
The same Rule that puts nothing before prayer also hands every monk a job, and it opens its chapter on daily work with a blunt sentence about a soul with nothing to do.

teach.h: IDLENESS IS THE ENEMY OF THE SOUL.
teach.b: Chapter forty-eight opens: idleness is the enemy of the soul. So, Benedict says, the brothers should be busy at set times with the work of their hands, and at other set times with holy reading. Tomorrow, the reading.
Today, the work: the kitchen, the garden, the fields, the workshop. And he doesn't treat it as a lesser thing tolerated between prayers.

teach.h: BY THE LABOR OF THEIR HANDS.
teach.b: When monks live by the labor of their hands, as the fathers and the apostles did, he says, then they are truly monks. Work isn't a break from the spiritual life; it's part of it.
But the Rule guards against the opposite trouble, too.
Everything should be done with measure, for the sake of the fainthearted. Brothers who are weak or delicate get work suited to them, so they're neither idle nor crushed. Not too little, not too much.
So the motto isn't really two separate commands.

teach.h: A RHYTHM, LIKE A GATE ON A HINGE.
teach.b: It's a rhythm, the day swinging between prayer and work like a gate on a hinge. Prayer keeps work from swallowing the whole person. Work keeps prayer from floating off into daydreams.
Ora et labora is a summary people use for that rhythm; the Rule's own sentence is the one about idleness.

Look back at the week: the tools of good works, obedience without grumbling, fewer words, the ladder you climb by stepping down, the seven hours, nothing before the work of God, and now the work itself, done with the same heart.
One house, one rhythm, from the chapel to the bean rows.

how: Benedictine monks and nuns divide their day between the hours of prayer, manual or other work, and sacred reading, and some monasteries support themselves through farming, crafts, teaching or guesthouses.

o: pray and work: the Benedictine rhythm
rest from work and give the day to prayer
work hard, and prayer will look after itself

s: in the Rule, work is a lesser thing squeezed between prayers
Benedict says monks living by the labor of their hands are truly monks.
Benedict asks that everything be done with measure, for the fainthearted
the weak get work suited to them, so they're neither idle nor crushed.
Benedictine monks only prayed and never worked
the Rule sets hours for manual work as well as prayer and reading.

games.q: you're the abbot. one brother is frail and can't keep up in the fields. what does chapter forty-eight ask?
o: excuse him from all work so he can rest.
give him work suited to him, so he's neither idle nor crushed.
keep him in the fields: work is work.
games.why: Benedict wants measure: the weak get suitable work, because idleness is the enemy, and so is a load that breaks them.

practice: Lay out the rest of today in your mind as a row of blocks, this job, then that one, and picture a small hinge between each: half a minute to stop, breathe and turn toward God, or toward stillness, before the next block starts.
Notice which block you most want to rush through, and put a hinge right after it. If you pray, make each hinge a short prayer you already know.

wordCard.voice: Ora et labora. Pray and work: the Benedictine rhythm in three words, with idleness as the enemy and measure as the rule. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: pray and work, a short summary of the Benedictine rhythm.

carryVoice: Your line: pray and work. A day that swings like a gate, instead of one long blur. That's the week.
